parrafos: In the schoolyard grew an enormous flamboyant tree.
No one remembered who had planted it.
During a cleanup, Elena found a plaque covered in dirt:
“Planted by the first class of this school.”
Intrigued, she visited the municipal library.
There she found a photograph of students from sixty years earlier next to a small tree.
Her grandfather recognized one of the boys: it was his brother.
Elena prepared an exhibit with the old picture and a current photograph.
When visitors saw both, they understood that the tree connected generations.
The principal proposed creating a record of the trees on the school grounds to preserve their history.
Elena learned that a community's identity also lives in the places its people take care of.
On the first day of school, Julián noticed an empty chair by the window.
The teacher explained that a new student would be arriving soon.
When Amira walked in, she spoke Spanish with a different accent.
Some classmates stood staring at her.
Julián remembered how he had felt when he changed schools the year before.
He went over, showed her where the supplies were, and asked her what games she liked.
At recess, Amira taught a circle game she played with her cousins.
The others shared their own games.
By the end of the day, the chair by the window no longer seemed like an unfamiliar place.
Julián understood that including someone begins with small actions: listening, inviting, and respecting.
Ariana visited a mangrove with her class.
The guide explained that its roots help protect the coast and serve as shelter for many animals.
During the tour, Ariana noticed wrappers caught among the roots.
She wondered how they had gotten there.
The guide explained that some trash is carried by wind or water from other places.
Back at school, Ariana drew a map showing the possible path of trash to the mangrove.
Her classmates organized a campaign to reduce single-use plastics.
They also requested proper bins for sorting waste.
Ariana discovered that caring for an ecosystem requires understanding what happens beyond its boundaries.

Mateo noticed that bottle caps intended for recycling were piling up in the classroom. They were hard to count and sort. He proposed building a simple machine with cardboard boxes and ramps. His first design mixed the large caps with the small ones. Instead of giving up, he measured the openings and adjusted the slope. After several tries, he managed to separate two sizes. At the school fair he explained the problem, the materials, the tests, and the changes he had made. Some visitors suggested improvements. Mateo wrote down each recommendation in his notebook. He had not invented a perfect machine, but he had made a solution he could keep developing. He understood that innovating means observing needs and learning from mistakes.

Every Friday, Sofía's group chose a snack to share. They almost always picked very sweet foods. One week, Sofía proposed including fresh fruit and water. Some classmates protested because they thought a healthy snack would be boring. The teacher suggested comparing options and checking the nutritional information with an adult's help. The group prepared fruit skewers, small sandwiches, and water with lemon slices. They also left room for foods that met different needs. On Friday, everyone tried something new. Sofía understood that taking care of your health does not mean imposing tastes, but learning to make informed decisions and respecting others.

A message appeared in the class chat announcing the cancellation of the field trip. It had no date and did not say who had written it. Pablo shared it right away and several classmates began to complain. Julia decided to check the information. She looked at the school's official notice and asked the teacher. She found out that the field trip was still scheduled; only the departure time had changed. Pablo felt embarrassed, but he corrected his message. Julia proposed a rule for the group: before sharing news, verify its source, date, and content. Her classmates agreed. They understood that the speed of a message does not prove that it is true.

Inés's grandfather took her to the town plaza during a cultural event. From one corner they heard plena; from another came the sound of a Puerto Rican cuatro. Near the fountain, a family was sharing stories about the celebrations of their country of origin. Inés wanted to listen to everything at once. Her grandfather explained that traditions change over time and are enriched when people exchange experiences. Inés talked with musicians and visitors, and wrote down new words in her notebook. When she got home, she drew a sound map of the plaza. She discovered that culture was not a single song, but many voices that could live together with respect.

At school, the students organized an art exhibition. They had placed the paintings on the second floor, which could only be reached by stairs. When Valeria noticed that her classmate would not be able to get there easily, she spoke with the committee. Some said that changing the exhibition would be too much work. Valeria proposed listening first to those who would face the difficulty. The group looked at the available spaces and moved the show to an accessible room on the ground floor. They also adjusted the height of several works so that everyone could appreciate them. On opening day, the exhibition welcomed families and students without leaving anyone out. Valeria learned that equal opportunity requires identifying and removing barriers.

After several dry days, Diego's neighbors noticed that the water from a community fountain was flowing with less force. Some thought it was a breakdown; others suspected the rain had decreased. Diego interviewed a worker from the water system and looked up information about responsible water use. He discovered that there could be different causes and that he should not choose an explanation without proof. While the problem was being investigated, his family fixed a leaking faucet and began collecting rainwater to water plants when it was safe to do so. Diego made a poster with practical tips. He understood that acting responsibly is possible even while answers are still being sought.

Nora's class received a challenge: to improve a space in the yard using available materials. One team wanted to paint a mural; another preferred to plant flowers. The discussion dragged on until Nora proposed creating an idea bank. Each group wrote down its proposal and explained its advantages and difficulties. They discovered that the mural would need a suitable wall, while the plants would require constant watering. In the end they combined both initiatives: they painted reused flowerpots and planted species suited to the place. When they finished, they put up a sign that said “Created by all of us.” Nora understood that listening to different opinions can lead to better solutions than a single idea.

Samuel wanted to win the school race. During practice he ran so fast at the start that he ended up exhausted. His coach explained the importance of warming up, staying hydrated, and keeping a steady pace. Samuel decided to practice with patience. He also began going to bed earlier the night before training. On race day he did not come in first, but he finished the course without stopping and improved his time. When he crossed the finish line, he congratulated his classmates. His coach reminded him that physical activity helps strengthen the body and that personal progress also deserves to be celebrated. Samuel understood that taking care of yourself is more important than chasing a victory at any cost.

During the school festival, Marina took a photograph of her classmates dancing. She wanted to post it right away, but she remembered that not everyone wanted to appear on social media. Before sharing it, she asked the participants and checked the school's rules. Two students preferred that their image not be shared. Marina respected their decision and chose to photograph the instruments and the decorations instead. Her post explained the event without identifying those who had not given permission. Later, a classmate thanked her for her consideration. Marina understood that a photograph can tell a story, but sharing it also means respecting people's privacy.

For her birthday, Camila received a small cloth doll from her grandmother. At first she had been expecting an electronic toy and did not know what to say. Her grandmother told her that she had learned to sew dolls with her own mother and that each one had colors inspired by family memories. Camila looked at the stitches and discovered that no two were alike. She asked to learn how to make one. For several afternoons they practiced together, making mistakes and laughing. When she finished, Camila gave her doll to a little cousin and told her the story of how it was made. She understood that some objects are valuable not for their price, but for the experiences and traditions they pass on.

On a field trip to the beach, the students were told to take all their trash with them. When they finished, Joel saw a bottle left near the sand. He thought it was not his responsibility because he had not left it there. Then he saw a bird approaching the object. He told the teacher and, following her instructions, picked up the bottle safely. The group checked the area and found other trash. Back at school, Joel proposed putting reminders in backpacks to reduce trash on future visits. He understood that protecting a shared place takes responsibility, even when the problem was started by someone else.
Once, a boy named Toñito went to school without knowing his lesson, and he was very worried, afraid that the teacher would ask him about it.
Toñito thought: “If only I could become invisible…!”

In the classroom, the teacher took attendance, and when he reached Toñito's name, Toñito answered: “Present!”, but no one heard him and the teacher said: “Too bad Toñito didn't come; I had been planning to ask him the lesson. I hope that, if he is sick, it is nothing serious.”
So Toñito realized he had become invisible, just as he had wished. In his joy, he jumped from his desk and landed in the trash can.

He got up and went around the classroom, pulling his classmates' hair and knocking over inkwells. There were noisy protests and endless arguments. The students accused one another, never suspecting that the culprit behind it all was Toñito the invisible.

When he got tired of playing like that, he left the school and got on a bus, without paying the fare, of course, because the conductor could not see him. He found a free seat and sat down. At the next stop a woman got on with a shopping basket and went to sit right there, since to her eyes it looked like an empty seat. But instead she sat on Toñito's knees, and he could barely hold her up. The woman shouted:
“What kind of trick is this? Can't we even sit down anymore? Look, I try to put the basket on the floor and it stays hanging in the air.”
There was a big argument and almost all the passengers complained bitterly about the streetcar company. But the basket was really resting on Toñito's knees.

Toñito got off in the center of the city, went into a pastry shop, and began helping himself freely, taking handfuls of all kinds of pastries and sweets. The saleswoman, seeing the pastries disappear from the counter, blamed a gentleman who was buying candy for an elderly aunt of his. The man protested:
“A thief, me? You don't know who you are talking to! You don't know who my father was! You don't know who my grandfather was!”
“And I don't want to know,” answered the saleswoman.
“How dare you insult my grandfather?” said the man, very angry.
It was a terrible argument.

Toñito the invisible slipped between the legs of the people there and headed back toward the school to watch his classmates leave. Indeed, he saw them come out, or rather, tumble down the stairs, but they did not see him at all. Toñito tried in vain to chase one or another of them, to pull his friend Roberto's hair, to invite them to play in the park. Roberto, to invite them to play in the park. They could not see him and paid him no attention; their gazes passed right through him as if he were made of glass.
Toñito went back home a little tired and a little discouraged. His mother was waiting for him, leaning out over the balcony.
“I'm here, Mom!” Toñito shouted.
But she could not see him and could not hear him, and meanwhile she kept looking anxiously at the street, waiting to see him appear.
“I'm here, Dad,” said Toñito, once at home, sitting at the table in his usual place.
But his dad murmured anxiously:
“Why is Toñito taking so long? Could something terrible have happened to him?”
“But I'm here! Here! Mom! Dad!” Toñito shouted.
But they could not hear him.
Now Toñito was crying, but what good are tears if no one can see them?

“I never want to be invisible again,” Toñito lamented, his heart broken into a thousand pieces. “I want my dad to see me, my mom to scold me, the teacher to ask me the lesson. I want to play with my friends.”
How awful it is to be invisible! How awful it is to be alone!
He went out to the stairs and slowly walked down to the street.
“Why are you crying?” asked a little old man who was sitting on a bench in the sun.
“But, can you see me?” Toñito asked anxiously.
“Of course I see you. I see you every day when you go to school and come back,” he answered.
“But I have never seen you.”
“Ah, I know,” he exclaimed. “Nobody notices me. A poor retired old man, alone, why would the kids look at me? To you I am like an invisible man.”
“Toñito!” his mom shouted at that moment from the balcony.
“Can you see me, Mom?”
“Ah! I wish I couldn't! Come on, come up and you will hear from your father,” she answered.
“I'm coming right up, Mom!” Toñito shouted, full of joy.
“Aren't you afraid of being scolded?” the little old man asked him, laughing.
Toñito threw his arms around his neck and gave him a kiss.
“You saved me,” he said.
“Eh, what an exaggeration!” said the little old man.

El original repite la frase 'Roberto, en invitarlos a jugar en el parque' (párrafo 13); se tradujo tal cual, conviene corregir la fuente. 'zafacón' se tradujo como 'trash can'.

quinto-es-01.titulo: The Lighthouse and the Two Proposals
parrafos: The town's old lighthouse had been closed for decades. When a plan to tear it down was announced, different opinions arose. Some neighbors wanted to build a parking lot that would make it easier to reach the coast; others defended the building's historical value. Valentina decided to do research before taking sides. She looked at photographs, interviewed fishermen, and asked specialists what work would be needed to preserve the lighthouse. She discovered that restoring it would cost money and require safety measures. At a meeting she presented a third possibility: to study its recovery as a cultural space and improve the parking in another area. Not everyone accepted the idea, but they agreed to evaluate its advantages and limitations. Valentina understood that community decisions get better when opinions are backed by evidence and different perspectives are heard.

Mariana was preparing for an academic competition when a classmate showed her photographs of questions that, according to him, would appear on the test. “We could win easily,” he said. Mariana felt a mix of excitement and worry. She had worked for weeks and wanted to represent her school well, but she knew that using those images would be unfair. She thought about staying quiet to avoid trouble. Then she remembered that her teammates trusted the team's honesty. She decided to talk to the teacher and explain what had happened without exaggerated accusations. The school looked into the situation and took steps to ensure a fair competition. The team did not win first prize, but Mariana came away satisfied. She discovered that acting with integrity can be uncomfortable and still be the right decision.

Javier visited a mangrove and discovered that its roots offered shelter to fish and birds, as well as helping to protect the coast. Days later he heard that building a parking lot near the site was being considered. Some residents thought it would make visits easier; others feared environmental damage. Javier gathered information about the ecosystem and asked neighbors about their needs. He understood that both groups were expressing real concerns, although they proposed different solutions. In his report he suggested evaluating existing access routes and consulting environmental studies before deciding. During the community meeting, he did not pretend to have all the answers. He explained what data he had found and what questions remained open. He learned that protecting the environment requires critical thinking, dialogue, and well-founded decisions.

Valeria wanted to find out what conditions favored the germination of some seeds. She prepared three containers with seeds of the same type, but changed the amount of water in each one. She recorded her observations for two weeks. At first she believed the dampest container would produce the tallest plants. However, several seeds did not germinate. Her teacher asked her whether she had also controlled the light and the temperature. Valeria admitted that she had not and that her conclusions were limited. Instead of hiding the mistakes, she included them in the report and proposed repeating the experiment. Her classmates valued the clarity of her explanations. Valeria understood that investigating does not mean proving that we are always right, but learning from the evidence.

A message began to circulate among students: “The school will eliminate all sports activities.” Many shared it without checking where it came from. Natalia noticed that it did not include a date, a signature, or a link to an official announcement. She asked her classmates where it had come from, but no one could identify the original source. Then she consulted the school administration and found out that they were only evaluating schedule changes because of maintenance. With the school's permission, Natalia wrote a clarification and explained how she had verified the facts. Some classmates felt upset about having spread the rumor. She avoided mocking them and proposed checking sources before forwarding information. They understood that a post can seem convincing and yet offer an incomplete or false version.

For a cultural fair, Elisa's group decided to research family recipes. Her grandmother shared a recipe for rice with pigeon peas; another student presented a traditional dish from his father's family, and a classmate explained a recipe she had learned from her neighbors. At first, some wanted to choose a single dish as the best. Elisa proposed comparing ingredients, the occasions when they were prepared, and the memories associated with each dish. They discovered unexpected similarities: many recipes brought the family together and required teamwork. They also recognized differences in flavors and customs. During the fair, each student explained the story of their dish without setting up hierarchies among cultures. Elisa understood that getting to know other people's traditions can strengthen appreciation for one's own.

A few days before a race, Samuel found an ad online promising to improve his performance with a miracle product. The message showed impressive testimonials, but did not explain where the data came from. Samuel was tempted to buy it because he wanted to win. Before doing so, he consulted his coach and his family. They talked about the risks of trusting promises without evidence and about the importance of rest, nutrition, and proper training. Samuel decided to stick with his training plan. On race day he did not take first place, but he improved his personal best. He understood that health should not be put at risk for quick results and that a responsible decision requires evaluating the available information.

The student council proposed painting a mural that represented the whole school. One group wanted to show only the most popular sports; another argued for including music, science, art, and family traditions. The discussion seemed to have no way out. Gabriela suggested listening to students from different grades and asking them what made them feel part of the community. The answers were varied. Some mentioned friendships; others, accessible spaces, cultural activities, or teachers who supported them. With that information, they designed a mural made of paths leading to a common plaza. No scene was the same as another, but all of them held an important place. During the opening, Gabriela explained that belonging does not mean being identical. It means finding respect and opportunities to take part.

During a visit to a rural area, Nicolás saw more stars than he could see from his city. He wondered whether the difference was due only to distance. He researched light pollution and found information about how certain lights make it hard to observe the night sky. He also read that lighting must be planned with people's safety in mind. At his school he proposed reviewing which lights stayed on when they were not needed. Instead of asking for all of them to be turned off, he presented alternatives: pointing lamps toward the ground and using appropriate schedules. His classmates analyzed the advantages and difficulties. Nicolás learned that a solid environmental proposal must consider evidence, consequences, and the needs of the community.

Irene and her classmates wanted to raise funds to buy books for the classroom. They thought of selling small plants grown in reused containers. Before starting, they calculated the cost of soil and seeds, asked families whether they wanted to take part, and agreed on reasonable prices. The first week they planted too many seeds and did not have enough room to take care of them. Irene proposed reducing the amount and organizing watering shifts. They also set aside some plants to donate to the community garden. At the end, the group reviewed how much it had spent and how much it had raised. They did not make a big profit, but they were able to buy several books. Irene understood that starting a business requires planning, responsibility, and attention to the well-being of others.

A photograph of Daniel looking the other way while his classmates cleaned the yard appeared on a social network. The text accompanying it said that he had refused to help. Several students began to criticize him. Lucía, who had been present, remembered that Daniel had stepped away to look for extra bags. The image showed only an instant and did not explain what happened before or after. Lucía talked with Daniel and, with his permission, clarified the facts. Then she proposed talking in class about how a photograph can be interpreted in different ways depending on the context. The students recognized that sharing images without enough information can hurt someone. They learned to ask, verify, and respect people's dignity.

Andrea's group was designing a school garden. They had chosen a stone path and several tall planters. During the presentation, Mateo explained that some parts would be hard to use for students with reduced mobility. Andrea felt frustrated: they had worked hard and she did not want to start over. Still, she decided to listen. Together with her classmates, she reviewed the plan, consulted accessibility guidelines, and changed the route. They also added spaces where everyone could take part in caring for the plants. When they opened the garden, Andrea understood that changing a project does not always mean failing. Sometimes it is an opportunity to make it fairer and more useful.

During a school activity, Héctor heard a bomba rhythm and wanted to learn its history. He found different explanations on various websites. Some were brief and did not cite sources; others included interviews with musicians and researchers. His teacher suggested that he compare the information and attend a cultural event where he could listen to people knowledgeable about the tradition. Héctor discovered that bomba is part of a complex history linked to Afro-Puerto Rican heritage and community expressions. In his report he avoided reducing it to simple entertainment. He included references to his sources and explained why it was important to respect those who preserve that tradition. He understood that studying culture requires curiosity, context, and recognition.

Alicia finished a novel whose last chapter did not explain what had happened to one of the characters. She thought the author had forgotten to close the story. Andrés proposed another interpretation: perhaps the ending invited the reader to imagine possibilities. In the book club, the teacher asked them to identify clues from the earlier chapters. Alicia found a letter in which the character talked about going back home; Andrés pointed to a conversation in which the character expressed a desire to travel. They each built different endings and defended their ideas with evidence from the text. Then they wrote a collective ending that combined elements of both proposals. Alicia understood that creating also requires listening, revising, and justifying decisions. The story did not have a single answer, but it had many opportunities to think.
